title: Divergent Determinants on Carbon and Nitrogen Exports From Major Arctic Rivers
content:
Abstract

Rapid Arctic warming plays a crucial role in changes of vegetation, hydrology and permafrost, substantially affecting the riverine carbon and nitrogen dynamics; however, their long-term trajectories and dominant controls remain uncertain. Here, by combining observations and model simulations in six major Arctic rivers, we estimate the changes and drivers of riverine carbon and nitrogen exports from 2001 to 2020. The dissolved and particular organic carbon (DOC, POC) fluxes show minor declines, NO3 −, NH4 + and particulate organic nitrogen (PON) fluxes remarkedly decrease, while total dissolved nitrogen (TDN) has a slight increase. Seasonally, DOC and PON peak in spring and summer, while inorganic nitrogen dominates in winter. Attribution analysis demonstrates that riverine organic carbon exports are primarily controlled by hydrology with the discharge exerting more than 50% control on DOC and POC fluxes, whereas nitrogen fluxes are co-regulated by interactions among permafrost, vegetation and climate. Specifically, NH4 + flux is mainly affected by vegetation (35.0%) and permafrost thaw (34.8%), NO3 − flux has the most important influencing factors of climate (38.6%) and discharge (38.3%), and PON flux suffers from the effects of hydrology (30.8%) and vegetation (19.1%). These findings highlight the divergent drivers for riverine carbon and nitrogen exports, providing critical insights into the Arctic land-ocean biogeochemical cycle.
